post.title: Contentsquare and AI-agent journey analytics
post.body:
Your next website visitor may be a shopping agent, not a shopper. Your analytics will need to tell the difference.

On October 13, 2026, Contentsquare announced a reimagined AI-first Experience Platform. Contentsquare says it captures human browsing alongside LLM and autonomous agent interactions, then separates and analyzes that traffic beside human sessions. It brings voice and text conversations, chatbot interactions, and agent dialogue into journeys as events. The platform also includes multi-session journey analysis, automated WebMCP monitoring, and multi-touch attribution that covers LLM- and AI-referred traffic. It is in beta for selected customers, with broader access planned in phases.

CDP Institute interprets the shift as brands managing two audiences: people and AI systems. Marketers may now need to consider both AI discoverability and what agents do after finding a brand. Those are marketing implications, not requirements from Contentsquare.

For marketers, that changes the job:

- Separate human and agent behavior in your event taxonomy. An agent adding an item to a cart may mean something different from a shopper doing it.

- Give AI referrals their own view in attribution. You can then see LLM-driven visits as a distinct source.

- Filter tests and anomaly checks by traffic type. A rise in agent activity could distort how you read a page or campaign result.

The takeaway: measure people and agents separately before deciding which journey needs work.

Could your analytics tell a customer from their assistant today?

topic.title: Facebook gives users direct control over recommendations

post.title: Facebook's Your Algorithm controls
post.body:
Facebook just gave users a steering wheel for its recommendation engine. Marketers should pay attention.

Meta's new "Your Algorithm" controls let users tell Facebook what they want to see more or less of across Feed and Reels. People can also set temporary topic interests, and Facebook says those choices will directly shape future recommendations.

This is bigger than a settings update. It is another step away from passive, black-box feeds and toward recommendation systems that users can actively train.

For marketers, that changes the job:

- Specificity beats broad reach. If users can explicitly choose topics, generic content becomes easier to tune out. Clear subject matter and a recognizable point of view matter more.

- Audience intent gets more visible. Topic controls can create stronger interest clusters, giving relevant content a better chance to find the right people, not merely the largest audience.

- Creative fatigue gets punished faster. "Not interested" is becoming a direct product input. Repetitive formats and bait-and-switch hooks may lose distribution more quickly.

The takeaway: don't build a content strategy around pleasing an algorithm you cannot see. Build one around being chosen by the people who can now help train it.

If your audience could directly tune your brand in or out, what would make them ask for more?

topic.title: HarrisQuest puts survey-backed brand tracking inside AI assistants

post.title: HarrisQuest MCP and survey-backed AI answers
post.body:
AI assistants know what the internet says about your brand. HarrisQuest wants them to know what customers said.

On October 15, 2026, HarrisQuest launched an MCP connector that brings its licensed brand and reputation data into Claude, ChatGPT, Gemini, and Microsoft Copilot. Teams can ask questions in the assistant they already use and get answers with the sample size, definition, and method attached. It is available now as an add-on to a HarrisQuest subscription.

The useful shift is not another chat window. It is primary market research moving into the same workflow where marketers draft briefs, compare competitors, and prepare leadership updates. HarrisQuest says the data covers about 200 interviews per brand each week across more than 4,000 brand-market combinations in 24 countries, with over 50 licensed metrics updated daily.

For marketers, that changes the job:

- Evidence stays with the answer. A brand metric is easier to defend when its sample and methodology survive the copy and paste.

- Research gets closer to action. Teams can turn a question into a saved view, report, competitive set, or audience segment and write it back to HarrisQuest.

- The guardrail is clear. The connector can create those outputs, but it cannot change the underlying survey data.

The takeaway: faster analysis matters when marketers can trace the answer back to the evidence. The shortcut should reduce tool switching without stripping away the audit trail.

If your AI assistant could query one trusted marketing dataset tomorrow, which one would you connect first?
